official_site.name: New York State Board of Elections

model_plain: Most New Yorkers vote in person, either during nine days of early voting (Sat Oct 24 to Sun Nov 1) or on Election Day (Tue Nov 3, 6 AM to 9 PM). Anyone can also ask for a mail ballot, but you must request one; nothing is mailed to you automatically.

deadlines.rule: Register or update your registration online by Saturday, October 24, 2026. The state calendar says the application 'must be received by BOE' by Oct 24, and the state deadlines page confirms Oct 24. Use the State Board of Elections online portal (elections.ny.gov) or the DMV if you have a NY license, permit or non-driver ID.

A mailed paper form must be received by your county board of elections by Saturday, October 24, 2026. Not postmarked: received. The state page says 'Applications must be received by a board of elections no later than October 24, 2026.' This late, don't mail it. Register online or go in person.

Hand a form to your county board of elections (or a state agency that offers registration, like the DMV) by Saturday, October 24, 2026. NYC BOE: 'Last day to register to vote in person is October 24, 2026.' Call your county board for Saturday hours before you go.

registration.same_day_notes: New York has no same-day registration. If you are not registered by October 24 you cannot vote on November 3. Separate from registration: the deadline to change your ADDRESS on an existing registration was Monday, October 19 (state calendar, Election Law 5-208(3); NYC311: 'Last day to request a change of address on your voter registration' is October 19). If you moved anywhere in New York after that, go to the poll site for your new address and vote by affidavit ballot; it counts and moves your registration. A 2019 law (Chapter 3, amending Election Law 5-208 and 8-302) extended this from moves within a county or NYC to moves anywhere in the state.
registration.still_possible_now: No. Registration for November 3 closed Saturday, October 24, and New York has no same-day registration. Check whether you're already registered at voterlookup.elections.ny.gov (NYC: amiregistered.vote.nyc, or call 1-866-VOTE-NYC).

mail_ballot.who_gets_one: Only people who ask. New York has two kinds and they work the same once you have one. Early mail ballot: 'Any registered voter may apply,' no reason needed. ABSENTEE ballot: for voters who will be away from their county (or away from NYC's five boroughs) on Election Day, have an illness or disability, are the primary caregiver of someone ill or disabled, are in a VA hospital, or are in jail or prison for anything other than a felony conviction. Same ballot, same deadlines. If you don't have an absentee reason, pick early mail. Apply online at elections.ny.gov/request-ballot (NYC: vote.nyc/RequestBallot), by mail, email or fax to your county board, or in person at your county board. 'Each person must apply for themselves.'

request_deadline.rule: Online, by email, fax or mail: the county board had to receive your application by Saturday, October 24, 2026 (state calendar: 'Last day for board of elections to receive application or letter of application by mail or online portal'). Apply in person at your county board through Monday, November 2, 2026, the day before the election. They can hand you the ballot to vote on the spot. The online and mail deadline has passed, so apply in person.

return_deadline.time: 9:00 PM ET if you hand it in

return_options: Mail it: 'Postmarked no later than November 3, and received by the County Board of Elections no later than November 10' (state BOE). Note: NYC311 says received by November 11; the state calendar and state BOE say November 10. Go by November 10.
Hand it to your county board of elections office by 9 PM on Tuesday, November 3
Hand it in at any early voting site in your county, October 24 to November 1, during that site's hours (NYC: any NYC early voting site)
Hand it in at any Election Day poll site in your county by 9 PM on November 3 (NYC: any NYC poll site)
Someone else can hand in your sealed, signed ballot for you
mail_ballot.postage: prepaid, statewide. State BOE: 'All early mail ballots include a pre-paid Return Envelope... The Return Envelope does not require any additional postage' (same for absentee ballots). NYC Votes: 'No postage needed!'
mail_ballot.signature_witness_rules: Put the voted ballot in the smaller security envelope (the state BOE's name for it; it has the signature line), then sign and date the outside of the security envelope and seal it. No witness or notary. If you make a mark instead of a signature, one witness must sign. Then put the security envelope inside the return envelope. A missing signature is the most common reason a ballot is set aside.
mail_ballot.cure_process: If your security envelope is unsigned or the signature doesn't match, the board must notify you and send a cure form; return it within the window on the notice and your ballot counts. Backstop: if you were issued a mail ballot, you can still go in person and vote an AFFIDAVIT ballot (not a machine). State BOE: 'If the voter's mailed ballot has been received, the affidavit ballot is not counted. If the mailed ballot has not been received, the affidavit ballot is counted.' Only one ever counts.
mail_ballot.mail_cutoff_advice: The state BOE passes along USPS advice to mail 'generally seven days ahead of the general election,' so mail by about Tuesday, October 27. Postmarks count, but USPS warns that a ballot dropped after the last pickup on Election Day 'will not be postmarked until the following business day,' which would miss the deadline. After Oct 27, hand it in: county board, any early voting site in your county through Nov 1, or any poll site in your county on Nov 3 by 9 PM.

early_in_person.hours_note: Nine days, Saturday Oct 24 through Sunday Nov 1. No voting on Monday Nov 2. Hours are set by each county. NYC (all five boroughs): Sat Oct 24, Sun Oct 25, Mon Oct 26 9 AM to 5 PM; Tue Oct 27 and Wed Oct 28 10 AM to 8 PM; Thu Oct 29 8 AM to 4 PM; Fri Oct 30, Sat Oct 31, Sun Nov 1 9 AM to 5 PM. NYC assigns you ONE early voting site, often not your Election Day site: 'You must vote at your assigned early voting site.' Look it up at findmypollsite.vote.nyc. Sullivan County (Callicoon): two sites, and 'All Sullivan County registered voters are eligible to vote at' either one: Sullivan County Government Center, 1st floor, 100 North Street, Monticello; and Sullivan County Public Health, 50 Community Lane, Liberty. Sullivan hours: Sat Oct 24, Sun Oct 25, Mon Oct 26 9 AM to 5 PM; Tue Oct 27 12 PM to 8 PM; Wed Oct 28 9 AM to 5 PM; Thu Oct 29 12 PM to 8 PM; Fri Oct 30, Sat Oct 31, Sun Nov 1 9 AM to 5 PM. Other counties: state BOE says 'Voters may visit any of their assigned Early Voting Centers in their county'; check your county board.

election_day.in_line_rule: If you are in line at 9 PM, stay in line. NYC311: 'If you are in line by 9 PM, you can stay in line to cast a ballot.'

accepted: Most voters show nothing: you sign the poll book (or e-poll pad) and your signature is checked against your registration
First-time voters who registered by mail without a NY driver license or ID number, or the last 4 digits of a Social Security number, may be asked for ID
If asked: a current, valid photo ID (driver license, non-driver ID, passport, student ID)
Or a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, or other government document showing your name and address
id_rules.no_id_option: If you're asked for ID and don't have it, you can vote an affidavit (provisional) ballot. It counts once the board confirms you're registered. Ulster County BOE: 'the voter will not be allowed to vote on the poll site voting system, but will be able to vote by affidavit ballot.'

in_the_booth.phones_detail: No state law bans carrying your phone or reading your notes on it at the poll site, and poll workers generally allow it. What's illegal is showing your marked ballot to anyone, and a federal court has read Election Law 17-130(10) to cover photographing it (Silberberg v. Board of Elections, S.D.N.Y. 2017). Many sites post 'no photography' signs and a poll worker can ask you to put the phone away. Keep it to reading your list. Source: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/ELN/17-130
in_the_booth.phones_short: You can read your plan on your phone; don't photograph your marked ballot.
in_the_booth.notes_detail: Bring a printed or handwritten list, a marked-up sample ballot, or this guide. The only limit is electioneering: don't show it around or hand it out within 100 feet of the poll site entrance (Election Law 8-104). Source: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/ELN/8-104 and https://www.nyclu.org/resources/know-your-rights/voting-new-york
in_the_booth.apparel_rule: No electioneering within 100 feet of the poll site entrance, including campaign buttons, hats and shirts for anyone on the ballot. Poll workers can ask you to cover up or take it off. An 'I Voted' sticker selfie outside is fine. Source: Election Law 8-104, https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/ELN/8-104

gotchas.text: October 24 was the last day to register and the last day to request a mail ballot online or by mail. Both have passed. You can still apply for a mail ballot in person at your county board through Monday, November 2, or vote early or on Election Day. No same-day registration in New York.
gotchas.short: Registration and online mail-ballot requests closed Oct 24; vote early or on Nov 3.

gotchas.text: The deadline to submit an address change was October 19. If you moved within New York since, use the polling place for your new address and ask for an affidavit ballot. Check your poll site before leaving.
gotchas.short: After Oct 19, vote by affidavit ballot at your new address's poll site.

gotchas.text: Nobody mails you a ballot unless you ask. If you want to vote by mail, request an early mail ballot (no reason needed). Once a mail ballot is issued to you, you can't vote on a machine in person; you'd vote an affidavit ballot instead, and only one of the two counts.
gotchas.short: To vote by mail, request an early mail ballot; no reason needed.

gotchas.text: Fusion voting: the same candidate appears on more than one line. Hochul is on Democratic and Working Families; Blakeman is on Republican, Conservative and Vote Affordable. Votes on every line add up for that person. Fill in ONE oval. Two ovals for the same person still count once; two ovals for different people in one race void that race.
gotchas.short: Fill in one oval per race, even if your candidate is on several lines.

gotchas.text: NYC: your early voting site is assigned and is often NOT your Election Day poll site. Check both at findmypollsite.vote.nyc. Early voting ends Sunday, November 1; there's no voting on Monday, November 2. NYC ballots also carry five ballot questions this year, all proposed City Charter amendments (NYC Votes: 'NYC voters will see five ballot proposals on their ballots'), usually on the back. Flip it over. There is no statewide ballot question in 2026.
gotchas.short: NYC: your early voting site may differ from Election Day's; flip the ballot over.

situations.question: I moved to a new address in New York.
situations.short: Go to the poll site for your new address and vote by affidavit ballot; it counts and moves your registration.
situations.answer: The address-change deadline was October 19. If you moved anywhere in New York since, go to the poll site for your new address and vote by affidavit ballot; it counts and moves your registration.
steps: Look up the poll site for your new address at voterlookup.elections.ny.gov (NYC: findmypollsite.vote.nyc).
Tell the poll worker you moved and ask for an affidavit ballot.
Fill in both your old and new address on the affidavit envelope.

situations.question: I moved out of New York.
situations.short: Register in your new state instead; some still take registrations or offer same-day registration.
situations.answer: You vote where you live now, so register in your new state instead. Some states still take registrations or offer same-day registration, so check today.
steps: Look up your new state's rules and deadline at vote.gov.
When you register, list your old New York address so your old registration can be canceled.

situations.question: I'm not registered yet.
situations.short: Registration closed Oct 24, but check first, because you may already be registered.
situations.answer: New York's registration deadline for November 3 was October 24, and there's no same-day registration. New voters can't register for this election. Check your existing registration before assuming you can't vote.
steps: Check first at voterlookup.elections.ny.gov. You may already be registered.
Not registered? Register now for future elections at elections.ny.gov, or through the DMV if you have a New York license or ID.

situations.question: The lookup can’t find me.
situations.short: The lookup needs your name exactly as registered: try your last name with the hyphen, a space, and joined.
situations.answer: New York’s lookup asks for your name, birth date, county and ZIP, and needs an exact match to your registration record.
steps: Try your last name with the hyphen, with a space instead, and run together, and leave out any middle name or suffix.
Still nothing? NYC: check amiregistered.vote.nyc or call 1-866-VOTE-NYC (1-866-868-3692). Sullivan County: call 845-807-0400. A failed search doesn't mean you're not registered; records can lag.

situations.question: I went to the wrong polling place.
situations.short: Go to your own poll site; an affidavit ballot elsewhere counts only in your county and Assembly district.
situations.answer: You need your own assigned poll site, so ask a poll worker to find it and go there if you can. If you can't, you can vote an affidavit ballot where you are, and it counts for the races you're eligible for as long as you're in the right county and Assembly district.
steps: Find your correct site at findmypollsite.vote.nyc (NYC) or voterlookup.elections.ny.gov.
NYC early voting uses one assigned site, which is often not your Election Day site.
Sullivan County early voting works at either site, Monticello or Liberty.

situations.question: My mail ballot never came, or I lost it.
situations.short: Online requests closed Oct 24; apply in person at your county board by Nov 2, or vote in person.
situations.answer: Check its status, then ask for a new one or vote in person. In person you'll vote an affidavit ballot, which counts as long as your first mail ballot never comes back.
steps: Track your ballot at voterlookup.elections.ny.gov.
Online requests closed Saturday, October 24. You can still apply in person at your county board through Monday, November 2 (Sullivan County: 100 North Street, Monticello).
Or vote in person during early voting (through Sunday, November 1) or on Election Day, on an affidavit ballot. It counts only if your first ballot never reaches the board.

situations.question: I made a mistake on my ballot.
situations.short: Don't scan it; ask a poll worker for a fresh one, or your county board for a new mail ballot.
situations.answer: At a poll site, tell a poll worker before you scan it and you'll get a fresh ballot, up to three in all. On a mail ballot, ask your county board for a replacement; if both come back, the one with the later postmark counts.
steps: In person: hand the marked ballot to a poll worker. Don't put it in the scanner.
For a new mail ballot, go to your county board in person by November 2; online requests closed Oct 24 (NYC: 1-866-VOTE-NYC; Sullivan County: 845-807-0400).
Or skip the mail ballot and vote in person by affidavit ballot.

situations.question: I got a mail ballot, but I want to vote in person.
situations.short: You can, on an affidavit ballot, which counts only if your mail ballot didn't reach the board.
situations.answer: You can, but you'll vote an affidavit ballot instead of using the machine. If your mail ballot already reached the board, the affidavit ballot isn't counted; if it didn't, the affidavit ballot counts.
steps: Go to your early voting site (October 24 to November 1) or your Election Day poll site.
Tell the poll worker you were sent a mail ballot and ask for an affidavit ballot.
Or drop your sealed mail ballot at any poll site in your county by 9 PM on November 3.

situations.question: I don't have an ID.
situations.short: Most New Yorkers don't need ID; if you're asked and have none, vote an affidavit ballot.
situations.answer: Most New Yorkers don't need one; you sign in and your signature is checked. If you're a first-time voter who is asked for ID and don't have it, you can still vote an affidavit ballot, which counts once the board confirms you're registered.
steps: If asked, a photo ID works, or a current utility bill, bank statement, paycheck, government check or government document with your name and address.

situations.question: My name changed since I registered.
situations.short: You can still vote: tell the poll worker, and sign with both names.
situations.answer: You can still vote. Tell the poll worker your name changed; you'll sign with both names and fill out a signature card that updates your record.

situations.question: I'm a college student.
situations.short: Online requests closed Oct 24; apply in person at your home county board by Nov 2, or vote early.
situations.answer: Registered at home but away at school? Online mail-ballot requests closed Saturday, October 24. You can still apply in person at your home county board through November 2. You can also name someone to deliver your application and pick up your ballot. Or vote early in person through Sunday, November 1.
steps: Already have your ballot? Mail it right away; it must be postmarked by November 3.
Registering at your school address instead closed October 24, so this year you vote where you're registered.

situations.question: I'll be away on Election Day.
situations.short: Vote early through Nov 1, or apply for a mail ballot in person at your county board by Nov 2.
situations.answer: Vote early in person any day from Saturday, October 24 through Sunday, November 1. Online mail-ballot requests closed October 24, but you can apply in person at your county board through November 2 and vote it right there.
steps: NYC: check your assigned early voting site at findmypollsite.vote.nyc.
Sullivan County: vote early at either Monticello or Liberty.

Already have a mail ballot? Don't count on the mail now: hand it in at any early voting site in your county through November 1, any poll site in your county on November 3 until 9 PM, or your county board.

situations.question: I'm in line when the polls close.
situations.short: Stay in line: if you're in line by 9 PM, you can vote.
situations.answer: Stay in line. If you're in line by 9 PM on Election Day, you have the right to vote.

situations.question: There's a problem with the signature on my mail ballot.
situations.short: Return the cure form the board sends you, in person or by mail; a timely postmark counts.
situations.answer: The board must tell you by mail, and by email or phone if it has them, and send you a cure form. Return it by the later of the day before the election or seven business days after the notice was mailed.
steps: Watch your ballot status at voterlookup.elections.ny.gov.
Sign and return the cure form in person or by mail; a timely postmark counts.
A missing or wrong date next to your signature doesn't need fixing if the ballot arrived on time.

situations.question: They told me to vote a provisional ballot.
situations.short: New York calls it an affidavit ballot; fill out the envelope completely, and it counts once you're confirmed eligible.
situations.answer: In New York this is called an affidavit ballot. Fill out the envelope completely; it's counted once the board confirms you're eligible, and the envelope also works as a registration update.
steps: If your name isn't in the poll book, ask for an affidavit ballot. Don't leave without voting.
Print clearly and fill in every line on the envelope.
After the election, call your county board to check on it (NYC: 1-866-VOTE-NYC; Sullivan County: 845-807-0400).

situations.question: How do I check that my ballot was counted?
situations.short: Track a mail ballot with the state's Mail Ballot Tracker; for an affidavit ballot, call your county board.
situations.answer: Track a mail ballot with the state's Mail Ballot Tracker at voterlookup.elections.ny.gov. For an affidavit ballot, call your county board of elections after the election.

judicial_review.how_judges_get_here: New York judges run with party labels. Supreme Court is the main trial court, not the state’s highest court. Parties nominate its candidates at judicial conventions.
judicial_review.who_reviews: Independent judicial screening panels and bar groups assess candidates’ qualifications. Look for a rating tied to the specific candidate and election.
judicial_review.what_the_rating_means: A qualification rating reflects that group’s screening for judicial office. Different bar groups can use different standards and reach different findings.
judicial_review.what_it_doesnt_mean: A qualification rating does not predict rulings. A party nomination is not a performance evaluation, and absence of a current rating does not establish lack of qualifications.
judicial_review.to_keep_a_judge: Vote for the candidate or candidates you want, up to the number shown on your ballot. These races do not use yes-or-no retention questions.
judicial_review.history: Some official screening-panel pages still show old ratings. Older ratings should not be described as a new 2026 review.
